name: Methodist Churches: Beginnings and Splits
summary: How Methodism grew from the Wesleys' Oxford Holy Club into separate churches in Britain and America, and divided over race, church government, slavery, holiness, and sexuality.
place: England and the United States, then worldwide

start.label: Charles and John Wesley's Holy Club at Oxford, mocked as 'Methodists'

end.label: About a quarter of U.S. United Methodist congregations leave over sexuality

key_dates.label: Christmas Conference founds the Methodist Episcopal Church in Baltimore
British Methodists begin giving communion themselves, separating from the Church of England
Richard Allen founds the African Methodist Episcopal Church
Methodist Protestant Church separates over bishops' power
Methodist Episcopal Church splits North and South over slavery
Holiness churches unite as the Church of the Nazarene
Northern, Southern, and Methodist Protestant churches reunite with a segregated 'Central Jurisdiction'
United Methodist Church formed; Central Jurisdiction abolished

background.text: Methodism began as a renewal movement inside the Church of England, with societies, classes, and lay preachers organized by John Wesley.

happened.text: After the American Revolution, Wesley ordained preachers for America, and the 1784 Christmas Conference founded the Methodist Episcopal Church under Francis Asbury and Thomas Coke.
Black Methodists, facing segregation in white churches, founded the African Methodist Episcopal (1816) and AME Zion (1821) churches.
Splits followed over lay representation and bishops (1830), slavery (1843–44), and holiness teaching (1860s–1900s); British Methodism also divided and reunited in 1932.
The United Methodist Church's long dispute over homosexuality ended in mass departures (2019–23) and the removal of its restrictions in 2024.

outcomes.text: Methodist and Wesleyan churches, including Holiness and (indirectly) Pentecostal churches that grew from them, have tens of millions of members worldwide.

persecution_note: Early Methodists faced mobs in Britain (see the Wesleys' and Whitefield's pages). In America Black Methodists faced discrimination within the church itself.

persecution.title: Black worshippers pulled from prayer at St. George's, Philadelphia
persecution.summary: At St. George's Methodist Church, white trustees pulled Absalom Jones and other Black worshippers from their knees during prayer for sitting in a section reserved for whites; Richard Allen, Jones, and others walked out, a step toward the founding of the AME Church and St. Thomas African Episcopal Church.

responsible.name: White trustees of St. George's Methodist Church

persecution.outcome: Allen founded Bethel Church (1794) and the AME denomination (1816).

sources.citation: Henry D. Rack, Reasonable Enthusiast: John Wesley and the Rise of Methodism. London: Epworth Press, 1989.
David Hempton, Methodism: Empire of the Spirit. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2005.
